extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, policymakers, and legislators considering administrative procedure and separation-of-powers reform
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly proposal for re-conceptualizing administrative law by doctrinally accepting legislative delegation and then reallocating administrative activities into legislative, executive, and judicial components with corresponding statutory/structural reforms. Includes concrete statutory text proposals for rulemaking, commission leadership, and adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept delegation as doctrinal reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Article argues that we ought to accept, as a functionalist matter, the delegation of legislative power to agencies and recognize that the administrative state exercises legislative, executive, and judicial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting delegation as doctrine allows use of formalist tools to delineate functions and to empower constitutional branches over the components corresponding to their functions; the Article emphasizes doing this only to the extent of historical practice (roughly eighty years) and not permitting novel, extreme delegations (e.g., to private parties or congressional committees). See discussion in Introduction and Part I (arguing acceptance of delegation will permit formalist solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineate administrative functions (legislative/executive/judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative actions should be classified and delineated into legislative, executive, and judicial components so that each constitutional branch exercises control over the component that corresponds to its constitutional function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where administrative action is 'mostly legislative' (e.g., prospective generally applicable rulemaking), Congress should have more control (including possible legislative veto); where 'mostly executive' (enforcement), presidential supervisory/removal authority should apply; where 'mostly judicial' (imposition of penalties affecting life, liberty, property), Article III review and judicial protections should apply. The Article acknowledges some activities defy classification and may require hybrid or negotiated solutions; classification should rely on precedent and functional characteristics (see Parts II and III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative veto constitutional when agency is making law
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislative veto of the administration’s legislative acts would be constitutional under the Article’s model when agencies are engaged in lawmaking rather than merely executing existing laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under modern doctrine a legislative veto is typically unconstitutional because agencies are treated as executing law (requiring bicameralism and presentment to repeal); but if rulemaking is treated as delegated legislation—i.e., lawmaking—then Congress can veto those legislative acts without bicameralism/presentment constraints. The Article discusses limits and possibilities for one-house vetoes and caveats (see Part II.A and accompanying subparts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking counts as lawmaking when prospective and generally applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking that issues prospective rules of general applicability should be treated as legislative in nature (rulemaking as legislating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article and cited scholarship (e.g., Kathryn Watts) argue judicial doctrine should recognize rulemaking as delegated legislative power in many instances; for such rulemaking, Congress should have legislative control mechanisms. The Appendix contains a proposed Administrative Procedure Reform Act §1 specifying procedural timing and congressional transmission requirements that operationalize when rulemaking is treated as lawmaking (e.g., transmit proposed rule to Congress by May 1; rule shall not take effect before December 1; presentation to President; treatment of congressional inaction and disapproval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rulemaking timeline and congressional transmission (Rulemaking Enabling Act proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed statutory procedural requirements for agency rulemaking to give Congress oversight and time to act before rules take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix §1 proposes: agencies must transmit a copy of a proposed §553 rule to Congress not later than May 1 of the year the rule is to become effective; such rule shall not take effect earlier than December 1 of that year unless otherwise provided; presentation to the President and procedures for approval, disapproval, and treatment of congressional inaction (inaction construed as assent but still requires presentation); if either house acts but no final bill is enacted, treat as no action; full-Congress resolution of disapproval prevents the rule from becoming law. These provisions operationalize when a rule is treated as legislative and subject to the Article’s legislative-veto framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential supervision and removal over executive functions (modified unitary executive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President should have supervisory and removal authority over executive functions of agencies and over independent commissions with respect to their executive functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional administration posits presidential administration is required as a constitutional matter for enforcement activities; the President is unitary with respect to administrative executive powers even if minimal or no control applies to agencies’ legislative or judicial functions. The Article proposes statutory mechanisms (see Appendix §2 Chief Commissioners) to implement presidential appointment of chief commissioners for independent commissions, four-year terms, and removal by the President; chief commissioners would prosecute offenses and exercise enforcement authority subject to presidential removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and duties for chief commissioners of independent commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory proposal for creation, appointment, term, removal, duties, and compensation of 'chief commissioners' for independent commissions engaged in enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix §2 provides specific text: President appoints chief commissioner with Senate advice and consent; four-year term; continues until successor qualifies; removable by President; chief commissioners shall prosecute offenses and civil actions to extent permitted by governing statutes; salary tie to Executive Level IV; Attorney General may appoint interim chief commissioner under conditions; oath requirement; staffing and appointment limitations. These are concrete design criteria for aligning commission enforcement functions with presidential control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: limit Chevron deference and analogize to presumption of constitutionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron deference to agency statutory interpretations should be significantly limited; courts should draw a parallel to the presumption of constitutionality when reviewing agency interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article argues constitutional administration justifies significantly limiting Chevron by treating agency statutory interpretations less deferentially—only to the extent courts believe interpretations are correct (see Appendix §3(c): 'the federal courts shall defer to agency interpretations of their governing statutes only to the extent the courts believe such interpretations are correct'). The Article also explains that recognizing delegation can change how courts treat deference in rulemaking contexts (see Part II.C.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo Article III review for traditionally judicial adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative adjudications that are traditionally judicial—those imposing criminal penalties, civil fines, or otherwise affecting life, liberty, or traditional property—should be subject to de novo review by an Article III court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article proposes that in any truly judicial adjudication, administrative law judges should submit reports and recommendations to Article III judges who must review both conclusions of law and fact de novo. This follows the magistrate/bankruptcy judge model; the Appendix §3(a) prescribes report-and-recommendation process, objection timelines, de novo determinations, and judges' authority to accept, reject, or modify agency findings, receive further evidence, or recommit to agency with instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative adjudication procedural rules (report & recommendation and objections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural requirements for adjudications that may determine private rights: agencies or ALJs must submit proposed findings and recommendations to a federal judge; parties may file objections; judge makes de novo determinations; parties may consent to agency final orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix §3(a) specifies: after an APA §554 hearing, agency/ALJ must submit proposed findings and recommendations to a federal judge; within 14 days any party may file written objections; judge shall make de novo determination of objected portions, and may accept/reject/modify findings, receive further evidence, or recommit; upon written consent of parties, agency may forgo these procedures and enter final orders. Appendix §3(b) extends these procedures to independent agencies and defines 'private rights' to include rights determined by common-law actions and deprivation of property by fine; §3(c) addresses deference in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards of judicial review for agency inaction (rulemaking vs enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Article contends that constitutional administration better explains why courts should apply different standards of review to agency inaction in the rulemaking context versus the enforcement context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, enforcement and adjudication (executive/judicial functions) may warrant different review doctrines than rulemaking (legislative function). The Article argues that recognizing the type of power exercised (legislative, executive, judicial) clarifies which review standard and remedies are appropriate (see Part II.C.3 and II.C.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit acceptance of delegation to historical practice and intelligible principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of delegation as doctrine is constrained: only recognition of existing delegations consistent with roughly eighty years of practice and judicial allowance; does not permit delegation to private individuals or delegation beyond intelligible-principle limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article rejects 'limitless delegation'—it clarifies that courts and historical practice have not sanctioned delegation to private parties or to congressional committees, and that what is accepted must fit within existing precedent (see Part III.C). The discussion references cases and scholarship about unacceptable delegations (e.g., Carter Coal, and recent cases on delegations to private parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize some administrative activities resist classification and permit hybrid controls
rubrics_metrics.description: For administrative activities that defy easy classification as legislative, executive, or judicial, Congress and the President may negotiate compromises and design hybrid controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article acknowledges not all administrative actions will fit neatly into the tripartite model; for those cases, existing compromises and statutory accommodations may continue. The model is primarily targeted at identifiable classes (certain rulemakings, enforcement, and judicial activity) where a confident characterization is possible (see concluding sections of Part II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-accountability and republican virtue: require agencies to consider congressional views
rubrics_metrics.description: Under constitutional administration agencies may need to take congressional views into account more often, shifting some political questions and deliberation to Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article frames this as a virtue for republican government: agencies' technical expertise will be treated as input while political valuation and decisions are made in Congress. This is a normative criterion for evaluating whether reforms improve republican accountability and mitigate interest-group capture in agency decisionmaking (see Part II.B and conclusion).
